section.heading: 11.7. Newton’s Method
Newton’s Method
section.paragraph: Previously, we have had occasion to find the zeros of a function $$f$$ or, equivalently, the roots of the equation $$f(x) = 0$$ . For example, the $$x$$ -intercepts of a function $$f$$ are precisely the values of $$x$$ that satisfy $$f(x) = 0$$ ; the critical numbers of $$f$$ include the roots of the equation $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ ; and the candidates for the inflection points of $$f$$ include the roots of the equation $$f^{''}(x) = 0$$ .

For linear and quadratic functions or for polynomial functions that are easily factored, the zeros of $$f$$ are readily found. In practice, however, we often encounter functions with zeros that cannot be found as readily. For example, the function

that gives the altitude (in feet) of a rocket $$t$$ seconds into flight (Example 8), is not easily factored, so its zeros cannot be found by elementary algebraic methods. (We will find the zeros of this function in Example 2.) Another example of a function with zeros that are not easily found is $$g(x) = e^{2x} - 3x - 2$$ . In this section, we develop an algorithm, based on the approximation of a function $$f$$ by a first-degree Taylor polynomial, to approximate the value of a zero of $$f$$ to any desired degree of accuracy.

note.heading: Newton’s Method (also called the Newton–Raphson Method)

list.item: Pick an initial estimate $$x_{0}$$ of the root $$c$$ .
Find a new estimate using the iterative formula (12) $$x_{n + 1} = x_{n} - \frac{f(x_{n})}{f^{\prime}(x_{n})} (n = 0,1,2,\ldots)$$
Compute $$\left| x_{n} - x_{n + 1} \right|$$ . If this number is less than a prescribed positive number, stop. The required approximation to the root $$x = c$$ is $$x = x_{n + 1}$$ .

section.paragraph: Having seen how effective Newton’s method can be for finding the zeros of a function, we want to point out that there are situations in which the method fails and that care must be exercised in applying it. Figure 12a illustrates a situation in which $$f^{\prime}(x_{n}) = 0$$ for some $$n$$ (in this case, $$n = 2$$ ). Since the iterative Formula (12) involves division by $$f^{\prime}(x_{n})$$ , it should be clear why the method fails to work in this case. However, if you choose a different initial estimate $$x_{0}$$ , the situation may yet be salvaged (Figure 12b).
